If within 4 hours of ingestion give activated charcoal. B

Obtain a stat acetaminophen level and with timing of ingestion, plot on the Rumack–Matthew nomogram to assess risk of hepatotoxicity and treat with N-acetylcysteine if in possible or probable range for hepatotoxicity. B
Treat with N-acetylcysteine if unclear history and signs of hepatotoxicity which could be related to the acetaminophen. C
Treat with oral N-acetylcysteine if ingestion is within 8 to 10 hours and patient is able to tolerate oral therapy. B

Treat with IV N-acetylcysteine if ingestion occurred more than 10 hours from presentation, if the patient is unable to tolerate oral treatment, or signs of hepatic failure. It is reasonable to choose IV N-acetylcysteine for patients presenting with acetaminophen toxicity regardless of time of ingestion due to tolerability, less gastrointestinal side effects, and shorter course of recommended therapy. background.definition: Acetaminophen (paracetamol or APAP) toxicity occurs when an acute dose, either intentionally or accidentally ingested, totals at least 150 mg/kg (about 7.5 g in adults) or when an acute dose produces an acetaminophen blood concentration that lies in the possible or probable risk areas of the Rumack–Matthew nomogram ().

list.listitem: Acetaminophen toxicity accounts for 10% of poisonings in the USA.

It accounts for more than 100,000 calls/year to poison control centers and more than 56,000 emergency room visits, 2600 hospitalizations, and an estimated 458 deaths due to acute liver failure each year.
Implicated in nearly 50% of acute liver failure cases in the US. Along with idiosyncratic drug reactions, acetaminophen has replaced viral hepatitis as the most frequent cause of acute live failure.
Acetaminophen toxicity has more deleterious effects on persons with alcoholism and appears to be further exaggerated by starvation.
Annual US cost associated with the toxicity of acetaminophen (excluding hepatoxicity) is estimated to be about $51.5 million.
Although acetaminophen is safe in therapeutic doses, it is widely available and commonly compounded with other medications increases its risk for accidental overdose or suicide attempt.

The cytochrome P-450 system converts acetaminophen to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine, which is toxic. It is conjugated with glutathione in the liver and is rendered inert. In high doses, the ability of the liver to conjugate acetaminophen is overwhelmed.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Other concomitant drug use that uses the cytochrome p450 system

list.listitem: Address basic life support first. C
Obtain a detailed history of time of ingestion, quantity and formulations. Early signs of intoxication include nausea and vomiting. C
Plot the acetaminophen level on a Rumback–Matthew nomogram to assess risk of hepatotoxicity (). B
Take a detailed history of exposure: time since exposure, amount of ingestion, number of ingestions, type of acetaminophen ingestion (long or short acting), and any concomitant ingestions.
Can be associated with increased risk of GI events.
Initial course of signs and symptoms (within hours): anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis.
Within 48 hours: liver enlargement, tenderness, and decreased urine output.
Within 3 to 5 days: jaundice, coagulation defects, hypoglycemia and encephalopathy.

Initial laboratory testing should include the following: acetaminophen level, AST and ALT, electrolytes, glucose, prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio, BUN, and creatinine.
The PT in particular has important prognostic value.
If clinically suspected, obtain beta-HCG to rule out pregnancy, salicylate level, and arterial blood gas.
A point of care test is highly sensitive and moderately specific for acetaminophen level greater than 25 mg/L.

A study of patients with rhabdomyolysis or acetaminophen toxicity found that those with acetaminophen toxicity tended to have lower AST/ALT ratios, with a cutoff of < 2.0 being 84% sensitive but only 52% specific.
Address ABC (airway, breathing, and circulation).
Obtain a thorough history and physical including time of ingestion, number of ingestions, amount ingested, and whether short or long acting preparations were ingested.

Check serum acetaminophen level. Plot, with time of ingestion, on the nomogram to determine likelihood of hepatotoxicity (). Nomogram is only useful with a single ingestion within 24 hours. The nomogram has high sensitivity for toxicity but low specificity ().
Check liver studies, international normalized ratio, renal function, and serum electrolytes.
Assess for concomitant exposure to other drugs and address appropriate precautions and psychiatric evaluation as needed.
Give activated charcoal if within 4 hours of ingestion. B
Treat with N-acetylcysteine if Rumack–Matthew nomogram shows probable or possible risk of the hepatotoxicity. B
Treat with N-acetylcysteine if ingestion history is unclear and patient has signs of hepatotoxicity that could be related to acetaminophen. C
Oral N-acetylcysteine if within 8 to 10 hours postingestion. B
IV N-acetylcysteine is reserved for patients unable to tolerate oral therapy, patients with hepatic failure, or patients who present for treatment more than 10 hours following ingestion. B
Those patients that progress to fulminant liver failure may benefit from liver transplant. B
Activated charcoal, 50 g given within 4 hours of ingestion to absorb acetaminophen remaining in the GI tract.
Treat with N-acetylcysteine if possible or probable risk of hepatoxicity by the Rumack–Matthew nomogram.
Treat with N-acetylcysteine if history is unclear and patient shows signs of hepatotoxicity or hepatic failure thought to be related to acetaminophen.

Oral N-acetylcysteine: Most effective if given within 10 hours of ingestion. Give 140 mg/kg (maximum dose: 15 grams) load then 70 mg/kg (maximum dose: 7.5 grams) every 4 hours for 17 doses. Patient must be able to tolerate oral therapy. Oral N-acetylcysteine may be associated with a foul rotten egg odor and taste as well as nausea.

IV N-acetylcysteine: Best if given within 8 to 10 hours. Loading dose of 150 mg/kg (maximum dose: 15 grams) in 5% dextrose over 15 minutes followed by 50 mg/kg (maximum dose: 5 grams) over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg (maximum dose: 10 grams) over the next 16 hours. IV N-acetylcysteine can be associated with anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, and seizure.

An alternative option includes the two-bag method over 20 hours. It has been associated with fewer and milder non-allergic anaphylactic reactions. The first dose is 200 mg/kg over 4 hours, and the second dose is 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. The maximum total dose is 30 grams.

IV N-acetylcysteine tends to be tolerated better than the oral formulation. It should be used in patients who have fulminant hepatic failure, or if treatment is begun more than 10 hours following ingestion.

Acetylcysteine therapy can safely be stopped when the patient’s acetaminophen level is undetectable, liver function tests are improving, and the patient is not encephalopathic. If the patient does not meet these criteria, an additional third intravenousbag (100 mg/kg over 16 hours) or 70 mg/kg PO q4h should bestarted until patient meets listed criteria.
Liver transplant is a consideration for patients who continue into fulminant hepatic failure despite medical treatment.
Artificial and bioartificial liver support systems as bridging to transplant are currently being evaluated for its efficacy and survival benefit.
A few other treatments have been suggested as possible adjuncts for prevention of acetaminophen-induced liver injury. These treatments have no current role in management of acetaminophen toxicity.
It is unclear whether first aid interventions by lay people are effective in limiting toxicity and saving lives in the pre-hospital setting for patients with acute acetaminophen overdose.
All suspected overdoses should be referred to an emergency department.
Poor prognostic signs include acidosis (pH <7.30), serum creatinine greater than 3.4 mg/dL (300 umol/L), and a PT greater than 100 seconds. These are known as the "King's Hospital Criteria." B
A model of end stage liver disease score of greater than 18 may be a useful predictor of fulminant hepatic failure. B
Poor prognostic indicators for patients with fulminant hepatic failure caused by acetaminophen include peak PT greater than 180 seconds and a continuing rise in PT on day 4. B
Acetaminophen use during pregnancy does not appear to be associated with higher risk of autism, ADHD, or intellectual disability.
Acetylcysteine can be found in cord blood.
However, there is evidence that pregnant women can safely be treated with N-acetylcysteine.

Adult preparation of IV N-acetylcysteine in children has been associated with hyponatremia and seizures due to excess free water and preparation should be adjusted for children less than 40 kilograms.

The volume of diluent is based on weight for children. Please see for information on how to dilute doses into the approapite volume of a compatible diluent. Compatible diluents include D5W, 1/2NS, and SWFI.

A systematic review of the safety of acetaminophen (paracetamol) in infants and children only found 52 studies demonstrating short-term hepatic safety (median follow-up of 48 hours), but no conclusive evidence for its safety on pediatric neurodevelopment, especially for cumulative exposure.
